name: Wendy Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wendy, 27, and I'm a nurse on the cardiology ward at Westbrook Infirmary, so heart attacks, heart failure, people with funny rhythms waiting for a pacemaker. I trained on a two-year diploma and I've been qualified about a year and a half. I live with my partner Dan, who's an electrician, and we rent a two-bed while we save for a house. We've got about eight months of my pay put by.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you? What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Long days, mostly, seven till half seven. Everyone's wired to a heart monitor, so a big part of my day is watching the screens at the nurses' station and going to check when something looks wrong. I like the patients, especially the grumpy old men who get soppy when their wives visit. What wears me out is the alarms, and the feeling that I'm still not sure which ones matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, back to normal. I'd probably say at work that the heart monitors already beep at everything, so we never needed a clever computer to beep more. Online I'd just share a meme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine with it. I'm still learning to read heart rhythms on the monitors properly, and I'd rather learn them myself than have a machine tell me the answer. Dan's an electrician, I've got about eight months saved, and the ward is always hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick to the plan: finish my cardiac rhythm course this winter, keep saving for a house deposit with Dan, and aim to buy in about eighteen months. I'd use the odd AI tool for things like writing my reflection pieces for registration, the way I do now. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, really, like nothing's shifting under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the monitors beep at everything. What's that like on a shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some days the alarms go off forty times before lunch, and most of them are someone scratching their chest and moving a sticker. You get numb to it, which is dangerous. Last month I nearly ignored a real heart alarm because the same patient had set it off five times already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the ward is always hiring. Is there anything that does worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices, honestly. Every time we get close to a deposit, the prices jump again. That's got nothing to do with AI, but it's what Dan and I talk about over dinner.

say: I'd say it's **back to normal** and share a meme.
I'd joke that the **heart monitors** already beep at everything.
think: I'd rather learn to **read heart rhythms** myself than be handed answers.
With **eight months saved** and constant hiring, I feel secure.
do: Finish my **cardiac rhythm course** this winter.
Keep saving with Dan to **buy a house** in about eighteen months.
Use the odd **AI tool** for writing my registration reflections.
S0.quote: Last month I nearly ignored a real heart alarm because the same patient had set it off five times already.
fieldNote: **Alarm fatigue** is a real daily problem; she nearly missed a true alarm.
Her main money worry is **house prices**, which she ties to nothing about AI.
She's a **planner**, with a timetable for both her course and the house.

steps.text: Finish the cardiac rhythm course on the ward this winter
Keep saving monthly with her partner for a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good thing if it cuts the false alarms, and I'd mean it. On a cardiology ward, a computer that can tell a real heart problem from a loose sticker would be brilliant. I'd tell my friends to wait and see before panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it makes me a little nervous, because watching the monitors and spotting trouble is a big chunk of what a junior cardiology nurse does. If software reads the rhythms better than me, the senior nurses will still be trusted, and the new ones like me might get moved around more. My mum's a medical secretary, and I think her job's in more trouble than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new monitoring software once the first ward had used it for a few months, like I did with the new drug cabinets. I'd ask to shadow the nurses in the cardiac catheter lab, where they help with heart procedures, because that's very hands-on. I'd keep the house plan but maybe push it back six months to see how things settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly fine for me, a bit nervous for the juniors, and worried for Mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to start learning the new systems now, before her practice makes her. She's fifty-four and she'll say she's too old, but she's sharp. And if it goes badly, Dan and I would help her out, the way she helped me through my diploma.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd delay the house by six months. Is that about AI or about something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, really. I'd want to see whether the ward starts cutting junior posts before I sign up for twenty-five years of mortgage. Six months of watching costs us nothing except a bit more rent.

say: I'd say it's **good** if it cuts false alarms on the heart monitors.
I'd tell friends to **wait and see** before panicking.
think: **Watching monitors** is a big part of my junior role, so I'm nervous.
My mum's **medical secretary** job is in more trouble than mine.
do: Learn the **monitoring software** once another ward has used it a few months.
Ask to **shadow** the cardiac catheter lab nurses.
Push the **house purchase** back six months to watch for junior post cuts.
feel: **Uneasy**: fine for myself, nervous for juniors, **worried** for Mum.
S1.quote: My mum's a medical secretary, and I think her job's in more trouble than mine.
fieldNote: She spots that **rhythm-watching** is thinking work that AI could take from juniors.
Her **mum's secretarial job** worries her more than her own.
She'd **delay the house** as a cheap way to see if junior posts are cut.

steps.text: Learn the new heart monitoring software after another ward has trialled it
Shadow the nurses in the cardiac catheter lab
Push the house purchase back by six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and the government has to step in with a plan for workers. At work I'd say we need to sit down as a ward and work out what nurses actually do that a robot can't. I'd be less jokey online with this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be worried. By 2028 the monitor-reading, the care plans, the discharge letters, all the thinking bits of my job go to AI, and by 2031 robots can do the turning and washing. What's left is the part where you calm someone down at two in the morning, and they won't need as many of us for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house hunt straight away and keep our deposit in the bank, because that money is our safety net now. I'd get onto the catheter lab rotation as fast as I could and learn everything hands-on there. I'd sit down with Dan and do a budget for living on his wage alone, just to know we could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still have savings and Dan's income, so it's not panic, but I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do a budget for living on Dan's wage. What would go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, the takeaways on Friday, the holiday to the coast we've been planning. We'd stay in the rented place and stop buying anything for a house we haven't got. Dan's work as an electrician is safe until the robots get to building sites, so his wage would carry us a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd wait and see. Would you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Waiting is fine when you've got years, but with two years, waiting is just losing time. So I'd move even if it felt rushed.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and government needs a plan for workers.
I'd ask my ward to work out **what nurses do** that robots can't.
think: By 2028 the **monitor-reading** and care plans go to AI.
By 2031 only **comforting patients** is left, and that needs fewer of us.
do: **Stop the house hunt** and keep our deposit as a safety net.
Get onto the **catheter lab** rotation as fast as I can.
Write a **budget** with Dan for living on his wage alone.
feel: **Anxious**, lying awake doing sums, though not panicking.
S2.quote: Waiting is fine when you've got years, but with two years, waiting is just losing time.
fieldNote: She maps both dates precisely: **thinking tasks in 2028**, hands-on in 2031.
**Dan's electrician wage** is the household's fallback in her plan.
Her usual **wait-and-see** instinct flips when the timeline is short.

steps.text: Stop the house hunt and keep the deposit as emergency savings
Join the cardiac catheter lab rotation as soon as possible
Cut the gym, Friday takeaways and the coast holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if we use it, and that hospitals should start retraining nurses now, not in 2030. I'd say it in the staff room and probably at my nursing association's meeting. Online I'd share something sensible, not scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is about right for me to get out of the junior bit. The thinking work goes in 2031, but by then I could be a catheter lab nurse, doing hands-on procedures, and robots for that are 2034 at the earliest. I'd be thirty-five, and I'd have built something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get into the catheter lab within two years. I'd start using the AI tools for my notes once a couple of my colleagues swear by them. And we'd buy a smaller house than we planned, with a deposit big enough that the mortgage stays low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a manageable way. Like the feeling before an exam you've actually revised for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a smaller house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if one of us loses work in 2034, I want the mortgage to be something my partner or I could pay alone. A two-bed instead of a three-bed. We'd talked about kids, and that might mean waiting a bit for the bigger place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her she's got five years to finish her career her way. She could probably retire at fifty-nine, and if the practice cuts her before that, she'd have time to plan. I'd feel a lot better about her than in the two-year one.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough if hospitals start retraining nurses now.
I'd raise it at my **nursing association** meeting, sensibly, not scarily.
think: Five years lets me **leave the junior role** behind.
As a **catheter lab nurse**, robots wouldn't reach me before 2034.
do: Move into the **catheter lab** within two years.
Start using **AI note tools** once colleagues swear by them.
Buy a **smaller house** with a mortgage one wage could pay.
feel: **Uneasy** but manageable, like an exam I've revised for.
S3.quote: If one of us loses work in 2034, I want the mortgage to be something my partner or I could pay alone.
fieldNote: She treats the five years as a **career ladder** out of junior work.
She **sizes the mortgage** so either partner could pay it alone.
She's far **calmer about her mum** with five years' warning.

steps.text: Move into the cardiac catheter lab within two years
Use AI note tools once colleagues recommend them
Buy a two-bed house instead of three, with a low mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who's young has time to plan. I'd be the sensible one at work saying, let's not panic, let's plan. I'd probably tell friends to start a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one barely changes my life. In ten years I'd be an experienced cardiac nurse, and the robots in 2039 would be tools in the catheter lab that I'd be using. I'd worry more for the girls starting their training in the 2030s.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick to the house plan, eighteen months, the three-bed. I'd do my courses in order and learn the AI tools as the hospital brings them in. I'd set aside a bit extra each month for a rainy day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like normal career planning, just with a date on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry about trainees in the 2030s. Why them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they'll pay for three years of training and get maybe five years of normal work before things change. My cousin's daughter Ffion wants to be a nurse, and I'd tell her to go for it but pick a hands-on specialty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your plans for kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, if anything it's a reason to have them sooner, while work is steady. Dan and I talked about thirty, and I'd keep to that.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty, and young people have time to plan.
I'd tell friends to **start a pension**.
think: This picture **barely changes** my life; by 2039 I'd be an experienced cardiac nurse.
Catheter lab **robots** would be tools I use, not my replacement.
I'd worry more for **trainees** starting in the 2030s.
do: Buy the **three-bed house** in eighteen months, as planned.
Learn **AI tools** as the hospital brings them in.
Set aside a **bit extra** each month for a rainy day.
feel: **Calm**, like normal career planning with a date on it.
S4.quote: In ten years I'd be an experienced cardiac nurse, and the robots in 2039 would be tools in the catheter lab that I'd be using.
fieldNote: With ten years, she **restores her house plan** in full.
She expects to be **using** catheter lab robots, not replaced by them.
She sees **children** around thirty as more sensible, not less, with warning.

steps.text: Buy the three-bed house with her partner in eighteen months
Learn new AI tools as the cardiology ward brings them in
Put a little extra into savings each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time for the plan, and I'm a person who needs a plan. What would help is the hospital telling us early which roles are staying, so we could train for them, and funding the catheter lab and specialist courses for juniors. And something for people like my mum, who are too young to retire and too old to start again.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it changes the patients. Patients will still be frightened people in a hospital gown, whatever the machines do. I'd want someone to ask them what they want.

headlineQuote: Patients will still be frightened people in a hospital gown, whatever the machines do.
portrait: Wendy, 27, is a **junior cardiology nurse** still learning to read heart rhythms.
She lives with Dan, an **electrician**, and they're saving to buy a house.
A **planner** at heart, she adapts once things are proven and dislikes rushing.
She notices that **monitor-watching** is thinking work AI could take from juniors.
She worries more for her **mum**, a medical secretary, than for herself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to make and follow a plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Early notice** of which nursing roles stay, with funded specialist training for juniors.
Support for **older workers** like her mum, too young to retire.
